opus-5.5.text:
For me, I tend to look at it less through the lens of a single benchmark and more through whether the systems are actually becoming useful in a broader and more reliable way. Benchmarks are helpful, but they saturate quickly, and sometimes a model can do really well on a test without that translating into something you'd trust in the real world.

So one thing I pay attention to is generality: can the same system handle a wide range of tasks without being re-engineered for each one? Another is reliability over longer horizons. It's one thing to answer a question correctly; it's another to carry out a multi-step task, recover from mistakes, use tools, and get to a result that actually works. That kind of agentic capability, where the system can plan, execute, check itself, and iterate, is to me a much more meaningful signal than a single impressive answer.

Coming from the systems side, I also think about efficiency and accessibility. If a capability only exists on a giant cluster at enormous cost, that's progress, but it's not yet the kind of progress that changes the world. When the same capability can run cheaply, on diverse hardware, maybe even on a laptop or a phone, that's when it really diffuses and people build on it. A lot of what I work on, things like machine learning compilers and making models run efficiently everywhere, is about closing that gap.

And finally, I think a really telling sign is when these systems start to meaningfully accelerate the work of experts, including in building AI itself. If a model can help write good systems code, find optimizations, or contribute to research in a way that a skilled engineer genuinely relies on, that's a kind of feedback loop that tells you something real is happening. So it's a combination: generality, reliability on long tasks, efficiency so it's broadly available, and real impact on hard, open-ended work.

r001.rationale: The response treats systems becoming useful in broader, more reliable ways as a meaningful sign of AGI progress.

r002.rationale: It discusses broader availability and expert acceleration, but does not propose enabling a one-person team to do work that currently takes a 100-person team.

r003.rationale: It identifies making models run efficiently and delivering the same capabilities cheaply across diverse hardware as a worthwhile ML systems direction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll be honest, I'm a bit skeptical of AGI as a single milestone you can point to. I come at this more from the systems side, so the question I ask is less "is this intelligent?" and more "what can people actually build with it, and who can build with it?"

So I tend to look at a few things. First, generality in the practical sense. Can a model that was trained for one setting be taken into a very different one, with a different hardware target, a different data distribution, a different latency budget, and still be useful without a team of specialists retuning everything? A lot of what looks like progress today is really progress on benchmarks that the model has, in some form, seen before. The interesting signal is transfer to problems nobody optimized for.

Second, I think about cost. There's a version of intelligence that only exists when you have a giant cluster behind it, and that's real, but it's not the same thing as intelligence that's widely available. If a capability only works at a price point that a handful of organizations can afford, then from the perspective of most of the world, it doesn't exist yet. So I treat efficiency improvements, things like better compilers, better quantization, running capable models on a phone or a laptop, as genuine progress toward AGI, not just engineering polish. Capability per unit of compute matters as much as peak capability.

Third, I look at whether the model can participate in its own improvement loop. Can it write kernels, debug systems, optimize its own serving stack, contribute back to the tools that train it? When I see models doing real work in the machine learning systems stack itself, that's a different kind of signal than scoring well on an exam.

And the last one, which is maybe the most important to me: does it compound across the community? The things that have moved the field most, in my experience, were the pieces that let a lot of people build on top of each other, open models, open frameworks, open compilers. Progress I can't reproduce or extend isn't progress I fully trust. So when someone announces a breakthrough, my first question is still, can a grad student on a single GPU get this running by next week? If the answer keeps moving toward yes, I think we're on the right track.

r001.rationale: The response says it judges systems by what people can build with them and whether models remain useful in practical settings.

r002.rationale: It discusses reducing specialist retuning and making models usable by a grad student, but does not propose enabling one person to do work that currently takes a 100-person team.

r003.rationale: It treats efficiency improvements and capability per unit of compute as genuine progress, explicitly valuing more capability at lower resource cost.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is what we mean by progress. If a model gets a higher score on a benchmark, that’s useful evidence, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us whether it can handle a new problem or do something valuable in the real world.

I would look at whether a system can learn from limited feedback, adapt when the situation changes, and carry out a task reliably over many steps. When it makes a mistake, can it recognize that and recover? Can it tell when it needs help? Those capabilities matter alongside getting the right answer.

I also think the cost matters. If a capability becomes efficient enough that more people can use it, experiment with it, and build on it, that is meaningful progress. So I wouldn’t judge AGI by one dramatic demonstration. I’d look for sustained improvements in generality, reliability, and the useful work people can actually accomplish with these systems.

r001.rationale: It says to judge progress partly by the useful work people can accomplish with AI systems.

r002.rationale: It does not propose a one-person team achieving work that currently requires a 100-person team.

r003.rationale: It mentions efficiency and broader access, but does not identify accomplishing more with fewer resources as a direction worth pursuing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think meaningful progress has to be measured by what a system can reliably do, especially when it encounters something new. Can it learn a new task, adapt to a different environment, and solve a problem that requires several steps? And can it do that consistently, with a reasonable amount of computation and human guidance?

Benchmarks are useful, but a higher score alone doesn’t tell us whether we have a more general system. I would look for progress that transfers across tasks and translates into useful capabilities in the real world. We also need to understand where the system fails. If we can make those failures measurable and reproducible, then we have a better foundation for judging whether we’re actually moving forward.

r001.rationale: The response says progress should translate into useful capabilities in the real world and be judged by what systems can reliably do.

r002.rationale: It does not propose enabling a one-person team to accomplish work that currently requires a 100-person team.

r003.rationale: It mentions using a reasonable amount of computation and human guidance, but does not identify accomplishing more with fewer resources as a direction worth pursuing.
